newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Presidents try to stem Central Africa bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Presidents try to stem Central Africa bloodshed.

text.p: African heads of state trying to halt a slide into ethnic bloodshed in the Central African Republic held lengthy talks on Sunday with soldiers leading the nation's third army mutiny of the year.

A spokesman for the mutineers said the presidents of Gabon, Mali and Chad, mandated by last week's Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso, had proposed a 15-day truce to allow experts to examine the problems and propose solutions.

The three leaders, plus President Blaise Compaore from Burkina Faso, held separate talks in the capital Bangui on Saturday with embattled Central African President Ange-Felix Patasse and all sides to the conflict.

The spokesman for the mutineers, who put the death toll on all sides at 150 since the latest mutiny began on November 16, told Reuters that Sunday's talks began at 11 a.m. and lasted late into the afternoon.

"The discussions were tough yesterday. They will continue on the non-negotiable points," Captain Anicet Saulett, leader of the mutineers, told Reuters by telephone before leaving for Sunday's talks at the French embassy.
He singled out as non-negotiable the resignation of Patasse and the departure of what mutineers say are Chadian and Sudanese mercenaries in his pay.
Compaore left for home before Sunday's talks started.

The latest uprising began over pay demands and an attempt by Patasse to redeploy soldiers involved in a May revolt but turned into an attempt to force Patasse to step down. The first revolt was in April.
Troops from former colonial power France, which intervened militarily in May to keep Patasse in power, guard strategic points in Bangui with presidential guard and army loyalists.
Bangui residents have reported a spate of tribal killings and abductions pitting southern Yakomas who dominate the rebel ranks against Patasse's northern Bayas.
Precise numbers have proved difficult to verify but victims include former interior minister Christophe Grelombe, a Yakoma, and his son, who were seized on Thursday and murdered.
Witnesses say the rebels, who control parts of Bangui, have suspended efforts to disarm Patasse supporters.
France's ambassador sat in on Saturday's talks with the rebels. Rebel sources said those talks lasted five hours.

Eleven opposition parties have signed a memorandum blaming Patasse for the turmoil and accusing him of ignoring accords that ended the May mutiny. "He is no longer in a position to embody national unity," they said.

Gabon's president, Omar Bongo, said after meeting Patasse on Saturday that Africans had to sort out the crisis. "The Central African Republic must not become another Rwanda, a Somalia, a Liberia or a Sierra Leone," he told French radio.

The rebels clashed on Thursday with loyalists and French troops protecting Patasse, who won multi-party elections in 1993. Bangui remained tense but calm on Sunday following isolated overnight gunshots. Markets stayed closed.
France has voiced backing for the elected government but says its troops based in the country under defence pacts would not help it combat the mutineers.
"French troops may only take part in maintaining order to avoid major abuses and protect foreign communities," President Jacques Chirac said on Friday after the Franco-African summit.
